text:
hey here is a convo i had, lets make a plan out of it for the game yeah so i was thinking about making an interface where i have the player model, i have all the joints as points i can grab, all the way down to the fingers and stuff, and then i will do some like keyframe stepping. also, one thing i was also thinking was just setting up my camera with some of those like vtuber style things have claude code one up to track my arms or whatever and then record animations like that 

Yeah, that is absolutely the right direction. You want an animation authoring workbench, not just a list of canned animations.

The clean version is:

Player model in center.
Skeleton/joints visible as grab points.
Timeline/keyframe strip at bottom.
Pose library on the side.
Live preview + onion-skin ghosts.
Record/capture button for webcam/body input.
Export becomes animation data: joint transforms over time, not code.

That fits the whole engine shape perfectly.

The manual joint editor gives you precision. You can grab shoulder, elbow, wrist, fingers, spine, neck, knees, feet, etc., and step poses across time. The important trick is to make it hierarchical: moving the upper arm carries elbow/wrist/hand unless you pin them. Same for leg/foot. Then you add constraints so it does not become hell: mirror left/right, lock feet, lock hand to item, keep elbow bending naturally, preserve ground contact.

So for a punch, you are not animating every bone from scratch. You set maybe:

idle pose
wind-up pose
extension/contact pose
recovery pose

Then the system interpolates, and you tweak the joints that matter.

For fingers, I would not start with every finger joint as raw freeform. That will get annoying fast. Use hand presets first: open, relaxed, fist, grip pistol, hold bottle, point, pinch. Then let you open the hand and fine-tune individual fingers only when needed. Same principle: structured authoring → flat animation data.

The VTuber/webcam capture idea is also very good, especially for rough blocking. Use camera tracking to capture body/arm/head motion, then turn that into editable keyframes. Not “perfect mocap,” more like “record a human gesture as a draft.” Then you clean it with the joint editor.

That workflow is powerful:

record yourself raising arm / aiming / stumbling / waving
retarget to character skeleton
compress/simplify into keyframes
edit joints manually
save as animation clip
chain clips in game

It also fits the motion-vocabulary idea we talked about. You do not need to author “entire long animations” as monoliths. You record primitives:

raise arm
lower arm
make fist
hold pistol
aim
reload
stumble
fall
push door
grab item
idle variations
drug wobble loops

Then gameplay chains them by reference.

For HMSC specifically, this becomes nasty because drugs, injuries, held items, and NPC suspicion can all consume the same animation layer. A “ketamine wobble” is not just a screen effect. It is a body animation modifier: gait instability, delayed arm correction, head lag, bad hand precision. NPCs can literally observe the animation signature: wobbling, stumbling, clipping, weird posture.

The data shape could be something like:

clip_id
skeleton_id
duration_ms
channels: joint → keyframes
events: contact, footstep, hit_frame, release_item
tags: intoxicated, aggressive, injured, stealth, visible_suspicious
constraints: left_hand_holds_item, feet_lock, look_at_target

Then the native host only needs a fixed animation system: sample clips, blend, apply constraints, emit events. The editor can be React and fancy; runtime gets packed animation curves.

The killer feature would be capture → simplify → reusable primitive. Record messy motion, then have the tool reduce it to a small keyframe chain. That keeps the game data tiny and editable instead of storing raw mocap noise forever.

I’d build it in this order:

First: skeleton viewer with draggable joints and pose save/load.
Second: timeline with keyframes and interpolation.
Third: clip playback on the character in-game.
Fourth: hand/item attachment presets.
Fifth: webcam/body capture as “draft animation input.”
Sixth: clip chaining/blending and animation events.

That gets you useful fast without drowning in mocap complexity. The manual editor is the ground truth. The camera capture is just a fast way to generate a first pass.

Yes, multiple cameras helps a lot. That turns this from “cheap 2D pose draft” into “actually plausible homebrew mocap.”

With one camera, you can track magenta dots well, but depth is ambiguous. With two or more cameras, you can triangulate the marker positions in 3D. You do not need fancy ML at first. You can do dumb color tracking + camera calibration + triangulation, which is way more in line with your engine anyway: fixed producer emits animation data.

The simplest usable setup:

Put two cameras at roughly 60–90 degrees from each other, both seeing the capture space. Front-left and front-right is good. Even better is front + side. Keep them fixed. Put magenta dots on joints. Record both feeds at the same time. Detect the same colored blobs in each camera. Match markers by label/position continuity. Triangulate 3D joint positions. Retarget to the character skeleton. Reduce to keyframes. Save clip data.

The calibration can start stupid simple. Put a known calibration object in the scene: a board, checkerboard, or even a few known marker points on the floor/wall. The system solves each camera’s position and projection. Once calibrated, a marker seen in camera A defines a ray into 3D space; the same marker seen in camera B defines another ray; the 3D joint is where those rays nearly intersect.

You can make the first version even less academic:

Use colored marker IDs instead of all magenta. For example shoulder = magenta, elbow = cyan, wrist = yellow, hand = orange. That avoids marker matching hell. If you want all magenta, the tracker has to infer identity by skeleton constraints and previous-frame position. That can work, but colored IDs make v1 way easier.

The capture pipeline should be:

multi-cam frames
color threshold markers
per-camera blob centers
marker identity matching
triangulate 3D points
fit skeleton pose
smooth/jitter filter
keyframe reduction
manual cleanup in joint editor
export animation clip

The nice thing is you can keep the raw capture as editor-only junk. The game package only needs the reduced animation data: joint rotations/positions over time, clip duration, tags, events. So even if capture is noisy and gross, the shipped clip remains tiny and clean.

The hard parts will be synchronization and occlusion. Sync does not need to be perfect at first if you clap/flash a light at start and align frames. Later, trigger both cameras together if possible. Occlusion is where multiple cameras shine: if the right wrist disappears in the front view, the side camera may still see it.

For HMSC, this is actually perfect because you do not need Pixar mocap. You need stylized physical behavior: walk cycles, stumble loops, aim poses, punch swings, drug wobble, idle fidgets, climbing, falling, “holding a bag,” “holding pistol,” “checking pockets.” That can be captured rough and cleaned.

The strongest version is a capture workbench inside ReactJIT:

left: camera feeds with detected markers
middle: 3D skeleton solve
right: character retarget preview
bottom: timeline/keyframes
button: record → simplify → save clip

Then the clip becomes just another producer output above the waist. Webcam mocap, hand-authored keyframes, JSON animation, or generated motion all compile to the same animation stream. The loader does not care where it came from.

So yeah — multiple cameras absolutely helps. You accidentally have the ingredients for cursed garage mocap. Which is, frankly, extremely on-brand.

interesting. so then the best thing would be something like say i wrap my fingers in a different color construction paper, and my hand with a dot on top and bottom and then do two tone or even three tone dots around my arm for both the lower and upper and do different tones to register it. that would work well, then i can just wrap like the handle of a stir stick and use that as like for a bat or knife or things and then i can use a broom for a two handed item like rifles. would be extremely low budget but the color tracking would be easy as hell at that point 

Yeah, that would work shockingly well for a v1. Honestly, the jank is the feature here: you are making the vision problem stupid enough that it becomes reliable.

The best version is not “track a human.” It is “track colored rigid markers with known labels.”

So instead of asking a model to infer fingers/arms from skin, shadows, sleeves, occlusion, etc., you make every important part scream its identity:

hand top marker
hand bottom marker
wrist marker
forearm marker A/B
elbow marker
upper-arm marker A/B
shoulder marker
finger colors or fingertip bands
prop markers on handle ends

That gives you enough geometry to infer bones and orientation, not just point positions.

For arms, two or three colored dots per limb segment is better than one. One dot tells you where the forearm roughly is. Two dots along the forearm tell you direction. Three dots around it can tell you twist/roll. That matters for things like aiming, holding a knife, gripping a bat, or turning the wrist.

For the hand, top + bottom dots is clever because it gives you palm orientation. Add a wrist dot and maybe a knuckle/finger-color band, and you can estimate hand pose well enough for game animation. You don’t need full finger mocap at first. You need “open hand,” “fist,” “grip,” “point,” and “trigger-ish grip.” Wrapping fingers in different colors could work, but I’d start with only thumb/index/pinky or fingertip color tabs, because all five fingers will occlude each other constantly.

For props, yes: a stir stick / broom / foam tube / cardboard knife shape with colored bands is perfect. Put one marker at each end and one orientation marker off-axis if you need roll. Then the system can solve the prop as a rigid body:

two markers = position + direction
three markers = position + direction + twist/orientation

That gives you bat swings, knife slashes, pistol-ish aim, rifle/broom two-handed stance, pushing, blocking, carrying, etc. The important thing is: keep the props safe and lightweight. You only need motion reference, not real force or real weapon handling.

A very practical marker scheme:

Use highly saturated colors that do not appear in the room: magenta, cyan, yellow, orange, blue. Avoid red if skin/lighting makes it messy. Avoid green if you use a green suit. Matte construction paper/tape is better than glossy because glare will confuse thresholding.

Use larger markers than you think. Tiny dots vanish with motion blur. For joints, use circles or square patches maybe 3–5 cm. For fingertips, little colored caps/bands are okay, but they need good lighting.

Give each rigid segment a unique color pattern, not just a unique color. Example:

upper arm: magenta + cyan
forearm: yellow + blue
hand: orange top + purple bottom
prop: red end + cyan end + yellow side marker

Then even if a marker disappears for a few frames, the system can recover from the pattern and skeleton constraints.

The solve pipeline can stay beautifully dumb:

threshold colors in HSV
find blobs
assign blobs to marker IDs
smooth positions over time
triangulate from multiple cameras if available
fit skeleton segment lengths
solve joint rotations
reduce to keyframes
manual cleanup
export clip

The constraints are what make it stable. For example: elbow must stay between shoulder and wrist; forearm length is fixed; wrist cannot teleport; hand top/bottom markers must remain near each other; prop markers have fixed distances. Once you add those, the tracker can survive occlusion and noisy frames without needing fancy AI.

And this fits your engine perfectly. The cursed cardboard mocap rig is just another producer above the waist. It emits animation clips. The game does not care whether the clip came from manual keyframes, camera capture, or a JSON file.

The smart first target would be upper body + props, not full-body walking. Capture:

idle variations
aim pistol / aim rifle
bat swing
knife slash
grab item
drink/smoke/use item
stumble/wobble drug loop
hands up / surrender
push door
fall/recoil

Those are exactly the animations that give HMSC personality, and they are much easier than perfect locomotion. Let locomotion stay hand-authored/blended first. Use garage mocap for gestures and item actions.

So yeah: green suit, colored construction paper, safe prop sticks, multiple cameras, dumb color tracking. Extremely low budget, extremely on-theme, and probably good enough to generate a huge animation vocabulary quickly.

kinda wild i just realized if i had a good setup i could easily turn this into a v tubing studio on the side, stream myself as a character while making the game lol 

Yeah, that realization is extremely real.

Because the mocap setup and the animation authoring setup are almost the same system. One pipeline gives you game animation capture; the other gives you live avatar driving. The difference is mostly whether you save the motion as a clip or stream it directly into a character rig.

So the same colored-marker / multi-camera rig can become:

capture markers → solve skeleton → retarget to HMSC character → render in ReactJIT/native scene → stream output

That is a VTuber studio.

And the hilarious part is that it would be dogfooding the engine while making the engine. You could be on stream as a character that is literally rendered by the same loader/data/animation stack you’re building. Then record the stream motions as reusable game clips. That is nasty.

The product loop becomes weirdly perfect:

You perform as the character.
The rig drives the avatar live.
The motion can be recorded.
The recorded motion becomes animation data.
The animation data ships in the game.
The game can be embedded back in the editor/stream scene.

That is the snake eating its tail again.

Also, HMSC has the right style for this. It does not need hyper-real facial capture. A stylized PS2/blocky/semi-gross character with expressive body motion, head turns, hand gestures, item props, and cursed wobble physics would be enough. The imperfections would read as personality instead of failure.

You could start with a very small “VTuber mode”:

webcam/multi-cam marker tracker
head/torso/arms only
mouth open/closed from mic volume
eyes/blink on timer or simple face tracking
hands from colored markers
prop markers for holding bat/knife/broom/rifle stand-ins
ReactJIT scene output as stream window

Then later: finger tracking, better face, multiple outfits, drug-state body filters, live scene switching, chat-driven effects.

The best part is that this would not be a side quest in the bad way. It would directly build the animation pipeline, character rig, item holding, camera system, and live rendering path. VTuber studio is just the editor-facing version of the same systems the game needs.

So yeah. You can stream yourself as a character while building the character system, and every improvement to the stream rig improves the game. That is a very good sidecar.
resolution: Produced the full-arc plan for the animation authoring workbench (USER convo: joint-grab pose editor, keyframe timeline, in-game clip playback, hand/item presets, garage mocap with colored markers, multi-cam/VTuber mode). Plan only — user explicitly chose no implementation this round. Plan saved at ~/.claude/plans/hey-here-is-a-delightful-pond.md. Key design: clips are the V6 'RLE/relational' format realized (sparse per-joint keyframe tracks + events/tags/constraints), exposed to the action DSL as an open 'clip' verb; pose editing rides buildRigFrameFromBones (the bones-are-the-pose seam); authoring extends the existing workbench ANIMATION context with POSE/TIMELINE/CAPTURE lenses; capture = Zig HSV blob tracker on the existing cam: CPU frame + ONNX pose assist per user answer. Six phases, strict order, each independently shippable.
